articles.title: ¿Cuántos feriados tiene noviembre? Revisa el calendario peruano 2026
articles.summary: Tras el feriado del primero de noviembre, te invitamos a conocer si hay otros feriados o días no laborables en el mes de noviembre. Conócelo todos en la siguiente nota.
articles.body_text: Los días libres son una oportunidad para compartir tiempo en familia, organizar actividades personales o realizar pequeños viajes sin las obligaciones habituales del trabajo. En noviembre de 2026, el calendario peruano contempla fechas de descanso que deben distinguirse entre feriados nacionales y días no laborables establecidos de manera extraordinaria. Estas últimas disposiciones están vinculadas con la visita del papa León XIV al Perú y comprenden jornadas y horarios específicos en Lima, Callao y otras regiones del país. Además, no todos los trabajadores tendrán las mismas condiciones para acceder a estos descansos, pues algunas medidas requieren compensar posteriormente las horas que se dejen de trabajar. Conoce qué fechas están previstas para noviembre, en qué lugares se aplicarán y cuáles son las diferencias que debes tener en cuenta antes de organizar tus actividades. El calendario de noviembre tiene un feriado nacional, el pasado 1 de noviembre, día de todos los santos, sin embargo; también cuenta con días NO laborables según lo indica la ley. Estas últimas fueron oficializadas mediante el Decreto Supremo N.º 020-2026-TR, publicado en el diario oficial El Peruano. El calendario contempla las siguientes fechas: La compensación dependerá del sector laboral. En las entidades públicas, las horas pendientes deberán recuperarse dentro de los diez días posteriores al descanso o cuando lo determine el titular de cada institución, de acuerdo con las necesidades del servicio. En las empresas privadas, empleadores y trabajadores podrán acordar cómo reponer el tiempo no trabajado. Si no consiguen llegar a un consenso, el empleador establecerá las condiciones para realizar la compensación correspondiente. Aunque ambas fechas permiten interrumpir las actividades habituales, tienen condiciones distintas. El feriado constituye un descanso obligatorio reconocido por ley y no requiere recuperar las horas que correspondían a esa jornada. En cambio, los días no laborables suelen estar dirigidos principalmente al sector público y contemplan la recuperación posterior del tiempo pendiente. Para los trabajadores privados, su aplicación depende del acuerdo entre empleadores y trabajadores. Según la Cámara de Comercio de Lima (CCL), si un empleado trabaja en un día feriado debido a necesidades de la empresa o rotación de turnos, y no recibe un día libre en sustitución, debe recibir una compensación económica equivalente a tres veces su salario habitual por esa jornada laboral. Esto se debe a tres conceptos: No cumplir con el pago adicional o negar la compensación de descanso constituye una infracción muy grave en materia laboral. Las sanciones económicas varían según el tipo de empresa, y pueden ir desde poco más de 1.000 soles hasta superar los 24.000.

articles.title: Fiscalía de Paraguay imputa y pide prisión para expresidente Peña por crisis bancaria
articles.summary: La Fiscalía de Paraguay solicitó este sábado que se ordene la prisión preventiva contra el expresidente Santiago Peña, al que imputó formalmente por presunta lesión de confianza y administración en provecho propio durante su comparecencia dentro de la investigación por el cierre de Ueno bank, una entidad a la que ha sido vinculado el exmandatario y cuyo caso provocó su destitución.
articles.body_text: La Fiscalía de Paraguay solicitó este sábado que se ordene la prisión preventiva contra el expresidente Santiago Peña, al que imputó formalmente por presunta lesión de confianza y administración en provecho propio durante su comparecencia dentro de la investigación por el cierre de Ueno bank, una entidad a la que ha sido vinculado el exmandatario y cuyo caso provocó su destitución. Peña fue detenido el viernes poco después de haber sido hallado culpable en un juicio político por “mal desempeño de funciones” tras la disolución por problemas de insolvencia de Ueno, un banco con 2,94 millones de clientes, entre ellos importantes instituciones estatales cuyos fondos quedaron congelados. Tras la solicitud del Ministerio Público, un juez deberá determinar, en una audiencia de imposición de medidas, si acepta el pedido de los fiscales. Según el acta de imputación, el exmandatario está acusado por presunta lesión de confianza como instigador y por administración en provecho propio en calidad de autor. El documento indica que el expresidente “habría intervenido en circunstancias relacionadas con la colocación, renovación y permanencia de importantes sumas de dinero provenientes de entidades públicas y previsionales” en Ueno bank, una entidad con cuyo grupo empresarial Peña “habría mantenido una relación económica y corporativa previa”. Peña era accionista de Ueno Holding, un conglomerado del Grupo Vásquez que poseía, entre otras empresas, a Ueno bank. En marzo de 2025 vendió esa participación, detalló la acusación de los diputados que promovieron el juicio político en su contra. Ueno bank, añade el documento de la Fiscalía, habría recibido esos recursos públicos “mientras desarrollaba operaciones crediticias con sociedades presuntamente vinculadas a su grupo económico”, en las que “fueron identificadas observaciones e irregularidades por parte de los órganos de supervisión del Banco Central”. El Ministerio Público también imputó y pidió la prisión preventiva contra el expresidente del Banco Central de Paraguay (BCP) Carlos Carvallo, por presunta lesión de confianza, producción inmediata de documentos públicos de contenido falso y administración en provecho propio, en calidad de autor. Carvallo se presentó en la noche del viernes ante las autoridades y fue arrestado. El exfuncionario presidió la Financiera Ueno, de la que nació Ueno bank, antes de asumir en 2023 la jefatura de la entidad emisora, cuyo directorio autorizó “83 días después” de su designación la creación de la finiquitada entidad bancaria, explicaron los diputados en su acusación. Durante la administración de Peña, el Instituto de Previsión Social (IPS), una de las principales cajas pensionales del país, invirtió unos 355 millones de dólares en Ueno, que también administraba las cuentas de unos 32.000 jubilados. Por este caso, la Fiscalía también ha imputado a 27 personas, entre ellas Miguel Vásquez, uno de los fundadores de Ueno bank, quien este viernes fue trasladado junto a otros cinco directivos a cárceles para procesados.

articles.title: Apps to distract you from the endless cycle of doomscrolling | TechCrunch
articles.summary: It's hard to break the cycle of doomscrolling, but there are plenty of apps that can help you spend more time on content that’s engaging and productive.
articles.body_text: You open your phone to check the time or a quick message. The next thing you know, an hour has passed and you’ve scrolled through endless celebrity drama, cat videos, awful news stories, influencer rants, and whatever else the algorithm decided to throw at you. Even though you probably don’t want to keep wasting your time and energy on this mind-numbing content, you do it again the next day. Doomscrolling, the habit of spending excessive amounts of time consuming content on social media, has become incredibly widespread. A survey from last year found that 64% of Americans say they doomscroll . Researchers have warned that doomscrolling can negatively affect several aspects of your well-being, including your mental health and attention span. Spending long periods scrolling can lead to brain fatigue, difficulty focusing, and disrupted sleep. And if a lot of the content you’re consuming is negative or stressful, it can leave you feeling disheartened , anxious, and emotionally drained. It’s hard to break the cycle of doomscrolling, but there are plenty of apps that provide content that’s engaging and productive. Of course, you could always read a book or go for a walk (we have a guide on how to stop doomscrolling ), but this list is for when you have a few spare minutes and want something to do on your phone that isn’t endless scrolling. Finch is a self-care pet app that’s designed to help you build healthy habits. You care for a cute virtual pet by completing small daily goals, such as drinking enough water, going on a walk, and practicing mindfulness. You can write about your day, complete a breathing exercise, or send good vibes to a friend by adding them to the app. The more self-care you do, the more your pet thrives. The app offers a fun way to trade mindless scrolling for small moments of self-care. Finch is available for free on iOS and Android . Libby is a free reading app that connects you to your local public library’s digital collection of ebooks, audiobooks, and magazines. All you need is a library card to borrow thousands of titles, which makes it easy to turn screen time into something productive. You can explore a new book during a commute or while waiting at a doctor’s office, turning moments when your fingers might otherwise itch to scroll into opportunities to read. Libby is available for free on iOS and Android .

articles.title: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy | TechCrunch
articles.summary: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
articles.body_text: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation . Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said. As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus . Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump , who’s been a cheerleader of the AI ( or “superintelligence” ) industry. In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel. In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers. Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies , including those offering sex or romance. articles.title: If Snap's Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they're also a lot more comfortable than they used to be | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Snap's Specs, which have been in development for many years now, are going to market this fall. Will they be a hit with users?
articles.body_text: When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood. Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway. What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had. Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable. However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless. I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were: By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases: Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases. The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. It’s an interesting product that — like a lot of its peers — doesn’t necessarily seem to have a clear purpose but, in time, could become many things. What the device currently offers, however, may not be compelling enough to encourage people to shell out the cash that Snap is asking for. articles.title: Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery. | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mystery solved: Coordinated power drops have been haunting power grid worldwide, but a team of researchers in Germany found the culprit.
articles.body_text: For years, mysterious electrical anomalies have been flummoxing grid managers around the world. Every 60 seconds, the frequency on the grid would drop a tiny bit. Even weirder: The sags happened at the exact same time on power grids across countries and continents. It was a mystery that Dirk Witthaut, a researcher at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany, couldn’t pass up. Germany’s largest transmission system operator, Tennet Germany, brought the puzzle to Witthaut, and it took years of investigative and modeling work to determine the cause. From Europe to Australia, the U.S. to Malaysia, the same pattern shows up in the data. Such frequency drops aren’t unheard of, but they are troubling. And the regularity with which they have been occurring can make the phenomenon feel even more ominous. The grid’s orderly operation relies on the frequency being kept within a certain range. If the oscillations get get too large, or if grid operators don’t know the cause and respond improperly, they can lead to blackouts. Even if the sags don’t cause blackouts, they can damage equipment in power plants if they go unchecked, especially in hydropower turbines. Hydropower plants have historically been a main driver of so-called ultra-low frequency oscillations (UFLOs). Every turbine vibrates, and if those vibrations occur with a certain regularity, known as the resonant frequency, they can magnify, sometimes to dangerous levels. Think of a wine glass breaking before an opera singer’s mighty pipes — that’s resonance. So Witthaut and his team started investigating hydropower, the most obvious potential culprit. They used a computer model of a hydropower plant control system on the Scandinavian grid to test the hypothesis. While they managed to find conditions that could generate a resonance that peaked once per minute, they couldn’t explain why it persisted for so long. Typically, resonances in mechanical systems will come and go, and so will the accompanying signal on the electrical grid. But this frequency drop kept happening minute after minute after minute. Every 60 seconds, without fail. It then dawned on the team that anything operating with such clockwork required, well, a clock. How else could they explain the uncanny timing? To that hypothesis, the researchers started close to home, installing more than 80 smart power quality meters around the Jülich campus. The research site is outfitted with medium- and low-voltage distribution lines, transformers, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems that serve as uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). It also has a high-performance computer system as well as the usual office computers powered by much smaller UPS devices. The power quality meters sampled a range of attributes, including frequency, voltage, current, and power, once every three seconds. Before long, the research team had its answer. The measurements recorded on the transformer attached to the battery energy storage system peaked every minute, just like on the bigger power grids.

articles.title: Sequoia partners reportedly blindsided when Roelof Botha joined SpaceX board | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A new report claims Sequoia's recent changes undo the legacy of the firm's former steward.
articles.body_text: Sequoia Capital announced some major changes this week, including the closure of its London office, the merger of its early-stage and growth teams, and the end of its Scouts program . Now, the Financial Times has published a report painting all of this as an attempt to undo the legacy of former leader Roelof Botha, who stepped down as the firm’s steward last year . An unnamed source told the FT that Botha “loved process and hierarchy,” while “the rest of the team didn’t.” Apparently, not everyone is on-board with the changes, with another source firing back that this seems like an “erasure of Sequoia’s heritage, not Roelof’s legacy.” The break between Botha and his old firm reportedly deepened after Botha joined the SpaceX board this summer. (Botha and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk previously worked together at PayPal.) A source told the FT that Sequoia’s partners were blindsided by the announcement, because Botha “didn’t ask compliance, he didn’t get sign off from the partnership” — even though his new role could complicate the firm’s ability to trade its $20 billion stake. A Sequoia spokesperson said that the firm continues to “collaborate closely” with Botha. articles.title: SNL has a new impression of Elon Musk, ‘the worst thing South Africa has ever done’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives.
articles.body_text: Saturday Night Live cast member Jeremy Culhane unveiled his impression of Elon Musk last night, depicting the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as an awkward loser who fumbles his attempt to befriend the hosts of Weekend Update. This isn’t the first time the show has lampooned the world’s richest man ( and one-time SNL host ), with Mike Myers dropping by occasionally to wield a chainsaw before freezing and muttering, “Glitch!” Since Musk was in the news this week for spending half a billion dollars on candidates who lost in the midterms , then announcing plans to halt Cybertruck production , it’s maybe not surprising that Culhane’s version is a little less obnoxious and a little more desperate to be liked, doing his best to laugh off his setbacks and remind the audience, “ My car did a flip !” Eventually, Weekend Update co-host Colin Jost asks a pointed question about Musk’s week: “You moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats. You moved all your companies to Texas because you didn’t want to pay taxes. You even built your own town in Texas. And now Texas is run by Democrats. Now you’re going to have to pay taxes. So how does that make you feel?” Culhane nods along with each step of the question, then answers, “Bad?” To show that he’s a good sport about all this, Culhane also asks his chatbot Grok to do “an epic vulgar roast of me, Elon Musk.” Grok delivers, describing Musk as “the worst thing South Africa has ever done” and suggesting, “Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you .” This week’s episode also featured a spoof of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” featuring Jane Wickline’s uncanny take on the Theranos founder (though most of the jokes focus on episode host Druski). SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives this season, starting with Wickline’s impression of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as a stuttering prophet of AI doom. A couple weeks later, James Austin Johnson caricatured data center backer/”Marty Supreme” co-star Kevin O’Leary . articles.title: He arrested a hacker, then spent 18 months clearing his own name. Now he’s a cybersecurity VC. | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Stephen Ward, a former Secret Service agent and Home Depot CISO, is preparing a second fund of roughly $250 million for Brightmind Partners.
articles.body_text: Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO. Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners , a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says. Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing. One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A . Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade. His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue. Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.” After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first. The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.) What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it. By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “ Operation Firewall .” Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: The Cybertruck experiment is over | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
articles.body_text: Almost seven years ago, while clutching a laptop, my phone, and a notebook in a sea of Tesla fans, I watched head designer Franz von Holzhausen throw a metal, baseball-sized ball at the driver’s-side window of the Cybertruck . The result was cracked glass — actually, two by the end of the presentation — and some awkward jokes and chuckling by CEO Elon Musk . I have witnessed a number of stunning, odd, and fantastical moments at Tesla events. But the Cybertruck reveal was the most interesting — and not because of the postapocalyptic design. It was the crowd. When the truck rolled out onto the stage, I watched attendees gasp, some in revulsion. There was mumbling (“This certainly can’t be the Cybertruck ?” I heard Tesla superfans whisper). And yes, there were cheers. The momentary shock of Musk’s biggest fans was quickly replaced by support, acceptance, and finally, endorsement. It moved like a wave over the crowd. By the time attendees were waiting in line for Cybertruck rides, the mood had shifted. Everyone was a fan. That fandom carried over to Cybertruck reservations, which skyrocketed to 1 million, Musk said during a third-quarter earnings call in 2023. But it never made the leap to actual sales. Industry experts estimate about 71,000 Cybertrucks have been sold since the first deliveries began in November 2023. And now the Cybertruck is headed to the scrap pile. Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, Musk said Friday. Was the vehicle too edgy? Maybe, but this was always going to be a niche market. I believe more practical reasons dampened sales. Musk promised the Cybertruck would have a 500-mile range and a price tag under $40,000. It achieved neither, senior reporter Sean O’Kane noted in his report . Zipline has had quite the week. Strike that — quite the year. The autonomous drone delivery startup, which was founded in 2014, has steadily scaled over the past few years. But 2026 has taken the company to new heights. In early 2026, Zipline raised $600 million and quickly added another $200 million to that Series H round. The company planned to use these funds to accelerate its expansion to at least four U.S. cities in 2026. Now it has even more money to grow even faster. Zipline announced this week it raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion. Electric truck startup Harbinger raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications. No word on the company’s valuation. Humble Robotics raised $51 million in a Series A round, bringing total funding to $75 million less than a year after founding. The round was led by Obvious Ventures with participation from insiders Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners, and others.

articles.title: Ninja's AutoBarista is impressively versatile, but one feature was a dealbreaker for me | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The AutoBarista's "Grind iQ" technology allows the machine to analyze your coffee beans to inform how it pulls a shot of espresso.
articles.body_text: I’ve made about a dozen different kinds of coffee drinks with the Ninja AutoBarista , and I have absolutely no idea what sort of grind size, tamping pressure, water temperature, or extraction timing is necessary to pull espresso shots for any of those drinks. The AutoBarista takes care of these considerations for you, making it possible to brew 13 different drinks with just the press of a button. The AutoBarista seeks to create the experience of having a coffee shop inside of your home, but without having to master the complicated, time-consuming nuances of making perfect espresso. It makes drip coffee and espresso-and-milk drinks, like cappuccinos or flat white. The fully automatic espresso machine can even make a pretty fast cold brew or cold-pressed espresso (just add ice, or else it’s more like lukewarm brew). The AutoBarista’s versatility comes from its “ Grind iQ ” feature. This technology allows the machine to pick up on your coffee bean size, roast type, and freshness, auto-calibrating the grind size, weight, and dose of each brew to make your drink of choice. As you customize the number of shots in your drink, the intensity of the shot, and the temperature, Grind iQ adjusts as well. If using something like Grind iQ sounds like bowling with the bumpers up, or playing Mario Kart with steer assist, then this is not a machine for you — stick with your pour overs and enjoy your gooseneck electric kettle. This is not a machine for coffee snobs who want to control every last detail of the brewing process. Rather, it’s for people who love coffee, but have never analyzed their espresso pucks. With the caveat that I am not invested in the coffee brewing process, I will say that I think the AutoBarista makes good drinks. On one side of the machine, it can pull shots of espresso or brew drip coffee, while on the other, it has an automatic milk frother and stainless steel pitcher, which allows you to customize settings based on your desired temperature and heaviness of the foam. It also includes a setting for frothing plant-based milk. To keep the coffee tasting good, the AutoBarista always rinses itself before and after making a drink. This is a useful feature — I often find myself manually running water through my Nespresso machine, since I don’t use it every day. But the water catches in a drip tray, which fills up after making just a few drinks, so if you live with another person, then emptying the tray will be a daily nuisance. While the design of the machine makes it easy to pull out the tray, I’ve accidentally overfilled it and spilled coffee-tinted water on my kitchen floor more than once. That’s the dealbreaker. When you pull out the drip tray, you’ll also see the knock box, which collects your spent espresso pucks. Be warned: if you forget to empty the knock box for even just a few days, you may get jump-scared by some blue mold next time you go to dump the pucks. Maybe I should’ve seen that coming, but scrubbing the moldy knock box made me feel ready to go back to my beloved OXO Cold Brew Coffee Maker , which costs just six percent of the price of the AutoBarista. In the AutoBarista’s defense, most people probably wouldn’t find this machine so arduous to care for. I just happen to be someone who makes one big batch cold brew every other week and tries to keep my morning rituals minimal. If you have more patience than I do before 8 AM, then you may very well love this machine and find it low maintenance. Ninja excels at making multi-use kitchen products, and the AutoBarista is no exception, combining a drip coffee maker, espresso machine, milk frother, and grinder, and food scale into one device. But if you’re not planning to take advantage of the AutoBarista’s versatility, then it’s not worth paying its $999.99 price. articles.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: On Equity, we unpacked what the midterms mean for the tech industry.
articles.body_text: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. articles.title: 3D DRAM created by IBM and Micron, 128GBps memory on the way
articles.summary: Smaller and faster RAM with up to 128GB transfer speed scould be on the way thanks to research from IBM and MIcron, using stacked chips and TSVs.
articles.body_text: Smaller and faster RAM with up to 128GBps transfer speeds could be on the way thanks to research from IBM and MIcron. The companies have developed three-dimensional memory, stacking individual DRAM chips vertically that would normally have to be placed side-by-side, though the efficiencies gained aren’t solely down to space. Communication between the stacked chips and the host device is achieved through a new creation known as through-silicon vias, or TSVs, which run vertically through the pile of chips and act as conduits to the host device. Thanks to the TSVs, in testing the memory has reached data speeds of 128GBps, ten times faster than current memory. On top of this, IBM claims the chips are 70 percent more power efficient than today’s DRAM. The new research is expected to form a key part of Samsung and Micron’s Hybrid Memory Cube technology, first announced back in October. IBM and Micron hope to have commercial availability in two years, with servers likely to use it first. Looking beyond that, IBM fellow Subu Iyer said that the new process “will have applications beyond memory, enabling other industry segments as well.” What exactly those new segments are remains to be seen, but we certainly wouldn’t complain if our computers got the kind of speed bump described here.

articles.body_text: JD Vance får hård kritik från egna leden angående att bli näste presidentkandidat. ”Det skulle innebära republikanernas undergång”, enligt en debattartikel i Trumpvänliga New York Post – och tidningens politiske kolumnist anklagar Vance för att ha ”förrått Trump”. En ”ökenråtta som demokratisk kandidat skulle kunna besegra Vance”, enligt Obamas tidigare rådgivare. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Donald Trump får som bekant inte ställa upp i presidentvalet 2028. Det spekuleras i att vicepresidenten JD Vance kan bli Republikanernas kandidat. Men det vore en mycket dålig idé enligt David Harsanyi, skribent på konservativa Washington Examiner. ”JD Vances katastrofala ekonomiska agenda skulle innebära republikanernas undergång”, skriver Harsanyi i en debattartikel i Trumpvänliga New York Post . Han pekar på hur mycket lägre förtroendet för hur Trump sköter ekonomin är nu jämfört med första mandatperioden som president, enligt opinionsundersökningar efter mellanårsvalet. ”Skyll den klyftan på vicepresident JD Vances inflytande”, skriver Harsanyi som menar att Vances ekonomiska politik ”inte har mycket till framtid”. New York Posts politiske kolumnist Michael Goodwin skriver att ”JD Vance förrådde Trump” med sitt ”oärliga” uttalande om Irankriget. ”Det är dags att vända honom ryggen”, skriver Goodwin. Vance får dock oväntat, men sarkastiskt, stöd som presidentkandidat i valet 2028 av Barack Obamas tidigare rådgivare Van Jones som ”verkligen hoppas att han ställer upp”.
